Title: Extending ALICE’s GPU tracking capabilities: Towards a comprehensive accelerated barrel reconstruction
Text:
Extending ALICE’s GPU tracking capabilities: Towards a
comprehensive accelerated barrel reconstruction
Matteo Concas1,∗and David Rohr1∗∗for the ALICE Collaboration
1CERN,
1211 Geneva,
Switzerland
Abstract. During Run 3, the ALICE experiment has enhanced its two-phase
data processing and reconstruction chain by integrating GPUs, a leap forward
in utilizing high-performance computing at the LHC. The initial ’synchronous’
phase engages GPUs to reconstruct and compress data from the TPC detec-
tor.
Subsequently, the ’asynchronous’ phase partially frees GPU resources,
allowing further offloading of additional reconstruction tasks to enhance the
reconstruction efficiency. Notably, the Inner Tracking System (ITS) [5] track-
ing has been ported as an independent module for two major GPU platforms.
This work will detail the integration of ITS GPU tracking within the existing
framework, aiming to develop a unified GPU-based reconstruction pipeline that
minimizes host-device memory transfer latency and coordinating various simul-
taneous processing stages. Performance metrics of the integrated system will be
discussed, highlighting the technical strategies and outcomes of this implemen-
tation.
1 Introduction
During the Run 3 at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the accelerator has been delivering
a rate of Pb-Pb collisions close to the nominal target: 50 kHz. The A Large Ion Collider
Experiment (ALICE) [1] has upgraded the majority of its sub-detectors [2] compared to Run
2. With its novel trigger-less data acquisition strategy, the "continuous readout", steadily
records input from every sub-detector. The stream of data is split along the time dimension
in so-called time frames of the duration of few milliseconds. To enable the study of very
rare physics signals, ALICE aims to record an integrated luminosity greater than 10 nb−1 of
minimum bias events. By the end of Run 3, the aggregated luminosity will eventually reach
50 times more minimum bias Pb-Pb collisions compared to Run 2.
ALICE faced many challenges in both hardware and software to support its data acquisi-
tion strategy. For this reason in Run 3, the ALICE computing model is built on a brand new
framework, rewritten encompassing both the online and the offline software in a single stack
called O2 [3]. The raw data input from the detectors is reduced from ∼3.5 TB/s in the First
Level Processing infrastructure, down to less than ∼900 GB/s. The online computing farm,
constituted by the Event Processing Nodes (EPNs), performs a detector calibration and data

reduction by means of data reconstruction. Such a reconstruction is split in two phases: the
synchronous phase performing the calibration and compression of the data simultaneously
with the data-taking and the asynchronous phase that operates the full processing of data pre-
viously staged on a temporary buffer. The usage of Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) greatly
boosts the computing capabilities of the EPNs. During the synchronous reconstruction, the
processing time is dominated by the data processing of the Time Projection Chamber (TPC),
which runs fully on the GPU. With the bulk of the EPN compute capacity coming from the
GPUs, the efficient usage of the GPUs is of paramount importance. Thus, all data transfers
are hidden behind computations using pipelines. Furthermore, the EPNs are equipped with
enough CPU cores and large enough memory for buffering, to feed data to the GPUs fast
enough to efficiently use their computing power. In the online processing, the processing on
EPNs is fully GPU-bound, and can reach 97% to 100% GPU utilization. During ordinary
data-taking operations, the fraction of allocated GPU resources slightly exceeds the required
amount of resources, so to have a safety margin to cover any issue.
The situation changes completely for the asynchronous processing. In this case, with the
full set of data from all detectors being processed, the GPU fraction of the total compute
workload currently ranges between 50% and 60% [4]. Thus, TPC is still very important
but other detectors are not negligible compared to the synchronous processing. The effi-
cient usage of remaining GPU cycles is a key point to maximize EPN compute efficiency
for asynchronous reconstruction. With only the TPC reconstruction performed on GPUs, the
graphics cards process only around half of the total workload, while providing 90% of the
EPN compute capacity. Consequently, the processing would be CPU-bound, with a lot of
wasted compute capacity on the GPUs. To increase the fraction of GPU compute workload
and the overall resource utilization, the tracking for the ALICE Inner Tracking System (ITS),
along with other detectors, could be ported to GPUs. These efforts will be described in the
next sections.
2 Upgraded Inner Tracking System data reconstruction in Run 3
The ALICE ITS is a brand new cylindrical silicon pixel detector counting more than 10 m2 of
sensitive area and a total of ∼12.5 billion pixels. It performs spatial measurement of charged
particles crossing the sensitive chips in the form of fired pixels. It is responsible for the iden-
tification of the interaction region and it is capable of tracking the charged particles produced
in the collision. It operates in the continuous readout data acquisition model, continuously
collecting a stream of data. Data recording is split in readout frames (ROF) by the detector
strobes: a hardware-paced time window containing ∼4.9 µs of data.
The reconstruction software includes a unified tracking algorithm for both synchronous
and asynchronous phases, which runs with different sets of configurations. During the syn-
chronous phase, the tracking is configured to reconstruct a fraction of the whole ITS data
stream (order of few percent) focusing on primary tracks, as they are instrumental for the
synchronous reconstruction process of the Time Projection Chamber (TPC) and to achieve
data reduction and compression. During the asynchronous phase, the ITS performs a recon-
struction of the full data, including shorter tracks from secondary decays and very low pT
(down to a few tenths of MeV).
3 GPU reconstruction in ALICE and the "optimistic scenario"
During the synchronous phase the fraction of the workload running on the GPU for TPC
reconstruction is greater than 99% [6]. During the asynchronous reconstruction, a signifi-
cant fraction of the GPU computing resources remains available for additional tasks to be

offloaded. In the so-called "optimistic scenario" ALICE plans to offload the reconstruction of
all the detector present in the barrel of the experiment on GPU this will eventually include,
other than ITS and TPC, the Transition Radiation Detector (TRD) and Time Of Flight (TOF)
and all of the reconstruction steps that involve combination of their reconstructed data, such
as the secondary vertexing. Measurements of the relative fractions of the compute workload
show that TPC requires between 50% and 60% of the processing time [4], depending on the
collision system and the interaction rate. Offloading this to GPU, eliminates 50% to 60%
of the CPU workload while being CPU-bound, yielding a speed-up of 2× to 2.5× as per-
formance peak. With the full barrel tracking on GPU, ALICE should eventually be able to
offload 80%, allowing for a total ideal speed-up of 5×.
The ITS is developing a GPU implementation of the tracking algorithm to be included in
this scenario. In 47 kHz Pb–Pb data of 2023, for instance, ITS tracking currently corresponds
to 12.5% of the total workload [4]. Running ITS on the GPU increases the GPU contribution
from 52.5% to 65%, increasing the ideal GPU speed-up from 2.1x to 2.8x. In contrast,
during synchronous processing, ITS workload represents only a tiny fraction of the total, as it
processes a only fraction of the data (∼1%), making it not worth to be offloaded to the GPU as
the I/O operations would not be negligible compared to the computation time. Even further,
since the GPU utilization can be close to 100% only from the TPC, moving more tasks to
GPU could even slow down the whole processing. Therefore, in the optimistic scenario the
GPU based ITS reconstruction is performed only for asynchronous processing.
4 ITS tracking on GPU
The ITS tracking algorithm for GPUs is described in [7]. It consists of a Cellular Automaton
phase that provides track candidates, followed by a track fit with a Kalman Filter. Finally,
the good tracks are selected, and used in the downstream processing for matching to re-
constructed information from the outer detectors. These steps are further subdivided into
sub-steps. It is ported to GPU in a modular hybrid implementation: providing the choice of
which steps to run on GPU to the developer in order to simplify the debugging.
The first phase running the Cellular Automaton has the highest memory consumption due
to the combinatorial nature of the algorithm. Memory consumption is particularly critical
for the GPU, since in order to fully leverage the parallelism, enough data must be processed
in parallel. Therefore, the ITS tracking partitions the available memory into chunks. Time
frames are divided and processed in these chunks. The processing runs with multiple streams
on the GPU, driven by Linux threads, each processing bunches of ROFs. All parallel in-
stances are almost independent of the others except for boundary readout frames, which can
be shared. This also enables for hidden I/O operations to run on one stream while kernel
executions are running in parallel on another stream.
Another important aspect related to memory is the sharing of the available GPU memory
between different detectors algorithms. For performance reasons, much of the memory must
be pre-allocated at initialisation time, and several buffers are filled with constants and cali-
bration objects. With multiple independent components, different detectors would compete
for GPU memory. The general ALICE GPU reconstruction framework thus provides mem-
ory management functionality, by preallocating all available GPU memory, giving chunks to
algorithms, and reusing the memory afterwards [8].
Initially, the ITS tracking was developed in a standalone way, to speed up the debugging
and testing. For that, it performed manual memory allocation and independent access to
GPU. Currently, it is fully integrated as an O2 GPU workflow, integrating steps within the
GPU main framework and using the shared memory allocation functionality.

The ALICE GPU paradigm provides flexibility in how to develop GPU algorithms. They
can be integrated into the global GPU library, or implemented as standalone pluggable library.
The ITS tracking is implemented in the latter way, which limits access to certain framework
functionalities but allows for still profit from existing instances of shared utilities. A notable
example features the usage of a common propagator interface class, provided by the GPU
framework, which abstracts the propagation of a particle track in the detector geometry and
updates the track definition accordingly. The same instance is share across the all of the tasks
running within the GPU reconstruction.
In order to still provide common components to external libraries, the GPU framework
was extended with an external provider CMake object library [11]. Examples are a fast
magnetic field approximation, material lookup table, and the propagator. The ITS tracking
integrated the external propagator as the first user, and thus served as test case for its func-
tionality.
The ITS tracking supports GPUs via the AMD ROCm [9] APIs and Nvidia CUDA [10]
programming APIs. The code base is plain CUDA, automatically translated to HIP at compile
time. The GPU framework automatically loads the requested backend enabling transparent
usage of CPUs and different GPU models.
5 Comparing results with the deterministic mode
A constant complication during the development has been that GPU and CPU results were
not 100% identical. This was usually accepted as being unavoidable due to the inherently dif-
ferent computing architectures. However, it was not clear whether the differences are caused
by concurrency or by bugs in the ITS tracking code. Therefore, ITS adopted the same strategy
as TPC tracking to implement an optional deterministic mode for debugging [11]. This mode
requires a recompilation and to adjust particular settings at runtime. While completely deteri-
orating the computing performance, it proved to be a potent debugging tool and has revealed
several bugs and hiccups. It is important to note that the deterministic mode requires 100%
identical results on the bit level at every reconstruction step. Otherwise, every tiny difference
will multiply and eventually make comparisons impossible, rendering the deterministic mode
useless. One example is for instance magnetic field strength passed in as double precision or
single precision floating-point value in an intermediate variable in the standalone version and
integrated version respectively. Even though the entire reconstruction code is 100% identical,
the tiny difference from the rounding at the very beginning will have effects on all tracks at a
bit-level. In corner cases, it will even lead to acceptance or rejection of tracks thus changing
the number and the ordering of tracks.
Figures 1 and 2 show comparisons of some track parameters, with the same input data
processed on CPU, AMD GPU with HIP, and NVIDIA GPU with CUDA, running in the
deterministic mode. These figures show perfect agreement, which has also been validated on
the bit-level.
6 ITS track fitting performance on GPU
In contrast to the Cellular Automaton phase, which splits the time frame into chunks, the
ITS track fit on GPU processes a full time frame at once. In Pb–Pb, a time frame requires
up to 300000 fits, requiring 500 MB of memory. On the CPU, ITS tracking runs with up
to 20 threads GPU has a larger horizontal computing scaling for the ITS fitting, as it usually
provides several thousands of threads, depending on the device specifications, which matches
the order of magnitude of the tracks that have to be simultaneously processed.

7 Secondary vertexing on GPU
The optimistic scenario 3 includes also the secondary vertex finding algorithm to run on GPU.
Notably, it constitutes 9% of the Pb–Pb processing time. Secondary vertexing targets the
reconstruction of vertices related to decay, conversion, particle cascades that can happen rel-
atively far from the interaction point. It requires the information related to the reconstructed
tracks of the decayed particles, and aims at reconstructing their originating point in space and
the parameters of the mother track that generated them. This is done by mean of a Distance
of Closest Approach (DCA) fit, a procedure that calculates the parameters of the mother track
at the position if closest distance of the two (or more) known daughters.
The DCA fitter is a well-established tool used in many places of the O2 code and is a cor-
nerstone for all the algorithm targeting secondary vertexing. It associates tracks using relative

ported to and is usable on GPU. Its only external dependency comes from ROOT with the
SMatrix class for symmetric matrices. A minimal copy of it is ported to O2. Its validation
is still pending since the class does not yet support the deterministic mode. It is currently a
proof of concept to use GPUs in more places, but has promising results already. Particularly,
it could be a first use case for GPU usage beyond machine learning also in Analysis. A first
toy demonstrator has already been used in a physics analysis as a proof of concept.
8 Conclusions
ALICE is successfully running the full TPC reconstruction on GPU during online processing.
ALICE is also one of the first LHC experiments that is using GPUs for GRID jobs [4]. The
next goal is to increase the GPU utilization during offline processing. The goal is to have the
full barrel tracking running on GPUs in a so-called optimistic scenario. This includes the ITS,
TRD, and TOF detectors as well as the secondary vertexing. ITS has a GPU implementation
for all steps of the track reconstruction. ITS Track fitting is the most critical part due to its
large processing time. Its GPU version shows excellent performance, while the other ITS
tracking steps are currently validated and benchmarked. A target for the first utilization of
the GPU based ITS tracking algorithm could be the reprocessing of 2024 Pb–Pb data, or 2025
data. Also the DCA fitter has been successfully ported on the GPU, which is spread across
many O2 use cases and is a critical component of the secondary vertex reconstruction. Its
adoption in some combinatorics-dominated physics analyses would be a nice by-product.
